power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Reliability-Aware Clinical Relation Learning for Uncertainty-Robust Multi-Label Chest X-ray Classification

author.affiliation:

text.text: Background: Automated multi-label classification of chest radiographs is complicated by overlapping imaging findings, noisy report-derived labels, and changes in disease co-occurrence across clinical settings.
Existing clinical-hierarchy methods can encode label relationships, but a rigid hierarchy may conflate categorical membership with empirical association and propagate annotation errors.
Methods: We investigated Reliability-Aware Clinical Relation Learning (ReCaRL), a graph-assisted framework for multi-label chest radiograph classification.
An image encoder produces initial finding scores, while a graph constructed from training-label associations provides reliability-weighted, confidence-gated updates.
Uncertain annotations are handled with observation masks.
The evaluation compares flat, weighted, graph-based, and hierarchy-penalty baselines, with internal and external discrimination and calibration assessments.
Results: In the internal evaluation, ReCaRL achieved macro AUROC 0.821 and macro AUPRC 0.437, compared with 0.812 and 0.423 for the masked/weighted baseline.
Mean AUROC across five common findings was 0.865 versus 0.858.
External testing yielded AUROC 0.799 and AUPRC 0.409.
Post-hoc calibration reduced the internal Brier score from 0.113 to 0.102 and the external expected calibration error from 0.082 to 0.061, without changing AUROC or AUPRC.

Conclusions: Reliability-aware graph propagation and confidence gating were associated with modest improvements in multi-label chest radiograph classification relative to the matched masked/weighted baseline.
Post-hoc calibration improved probability reliability in the reported evaluations.
The findings do not establish a benefit in prospective clinical decision-making.
Chest radiography is a high-volume examination used to assess diverse cardiopulmonary findings, including atelectasis, consolidation, edema, cardiomegaly, and pleural effusion.
Contemporary public datasets have enabled the development of multi-label image classifiers at scale.
CheXpert contains 224,316 chest radiographs from 65,240 patients and provides report-derived labels that distinguish positive, negative, and uncertain observations [1].
text.formatted: CheXpert contains 224,316 chest radiographs from 65,240 patients and provides report-derived labels that distinguish positive, negative, and uncertain observations <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: MIMIC-CXR includes 377,110 radiographs across 227,835 studies with accompanying radiology reports and provides an important independent institutional setting for model assessment [2].
text.formatted: MIMIC-CXR includes 377,110 radiographs across 227,835 studies with accompanying radiology reports and provides an important independent institutional setting for model assessment <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: Multi-label CXR prediction differs from a collection of unrelated binary tasks because findings may coexist and may be linked by anatomical or semantic structure.
However, not all clinical relationships are equivalent.

Categorical membership can be definitional (for example, pleural effusion belongs to a pleuralfinding group), whereas associations among edema, effusion, and cardiomegaly are population-dependent and do not imply deterministic disease relationships.
Directly converting such associations into hard parent-child constraints risks creating inconsistent targets or amplifying spurious correlations in unfamiliar patient populations.
A recent clinically inspired hierarchical approach combined DenseNet121 with a penalty-based hierarchical binary cross-entropy objective [3].
text.formatted: A recent clinically inspired hierarchical approach combined DenseNet121 with a penalty-based hierarchical binary cross-entropy objective <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: Earlier work also formulated conditional and unconditional predictions within chest radiograph taxonomies and examined learning from incomplete annotations [15].
text.formatted: Earlier work also formulated conditional and unconditional predictions within chest radiograph taxonomies and examined learning from incomplete annotations <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>.

text.text: Its reported overall hierarchy-level mean AUROC was approximately 0.903; notably, the original paper also reported a five-label flat model that performed better than several hierarchy-penalty configurations [3].
text.formatted: Its reported overall hierarchy-level mean AUROC was approximately 0.903; notably, the original paper also reported a five-label flat model that performed better than several hierarchy-penalty configurations <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: This distinction motivates a narrower question: can models obtain useful contextual information from co-occurring findings without treating every observed association as a necessary clinical implication?

Chest radiograph foundation models such as CheXFound and Ark+ have expanded the range of transferable image representations [4, 5], and data-efficient vision-language pretraining offers another route to learning from paired radiographs and reports [6].
text.formatted: Chest radiograph foundation models such as CheXFound and Ark+ have expanded the range of transferable image representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5]</ref>, and data-efficient vision-language pretraining offers another route to learning from paired radiographs and reports <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: Complementary research has linked narrative findings to localized image evidence through report-guided segmentation [11] and combined radiographic interpretation with report-conditioned evidence generation in a shared world-model representation [12].
text.formatted: Complementary research has linked narrative findings to localized image evidence through report-guided segmentation <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> and combined radiographic interpretation with report-conditioned evidence generation in a shared world-model representation <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: Although these developments address increasingly complex aspects of visual understanding, they do not directly establish whether empirical dependencies among disease labels are sufficiently reliable to improve calibrated multi-label classification across institutions.
Transparent evaluation and clearly defined reference standards therefore remain essential [7, 8].
text.formatted: Transparent evaluation and clearly defined reference standards therefore remain essential <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8]</ref>.

text.text: We investigate Reliability-Aware Clinical Relation Learning (ReCaRL) as a means of distinguishing descriptive clinical groupings from statistical label associations.
The model downweights edges with limited support or weak resampling stability and attenuates messages from uncertain source predictions.
Ambiguous report-derived labels are handled as incompletely observed targets rather than automatically assigned to the negative class.
These design choices address a specific question: whether estimated relationships among findings can be used without treating each association as a deterministic implication.
Multi-label CXR classifiers have modeled dependencies using co-occurrence statistics, semantic graphs, and clinically organized taxonomies [3, 9, 15].
text.formatted: Multi-label CXR classifiers have modeled dependencies using co-occurrence statistics, semantic graphs, and clinically organized taxonomies <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15]</ref>.

text.text: Such methods exploit shared information among findings, but empirical associations depend on disease prevalence, clinical practice, and report-labeling conventions.

In a related task, Xi et al. used radiology reports to guide spatial delineation of findings, illustrating the importance of preserving correspondence between clinical descriptions and image evidence [11].
text.formatted: In a related task, Xi et al. used radiology reports to guide spatial delineation of findings, illustrating the importance of preserving correspondence between clinical descriptions and image evidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>.

text.text: ReCaRL examines label-to-label association reliability rather than report-grounded localization.
The hierarchical penalty-based framework [3] provides a relevant reference method for the comparison.
text.formatted: The hierarchical penalty-based framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> provides a relevant reference method for the comparison.

text.text: CheXpert annotations distinguish positive, negative, uncertain, and unmentioned observations extracted from reports [1].
text.formatted: CheXpert annotations distinguish positive, negative, uncertain, and unmentioned observations extracted from reports <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: CheXbert demonstrated the use of language-model-based report labeling, while VisualCheXbert showed that labels inferred from reports may differ from findings adjudicated directly from radiographs [16, 17].
text.formatted: CheXbert demonstrated the use of language-model-based report labeling, while VisualCheXbert showed that labels inferred from reports may differ from findings adjudicated directly from radiographs <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17]</ref>.

text.text: Uncertain mentions are not verified negatives, while unmentioned findings may reflect reporting conventions rather than true absence.
A review of uncertainty in medical imaging AI emphasized the distinction between predictive uncertainty, confidence, and calibration [13].
text.formatted: A review of uncertainty in medical imaging AI emphasized the distinction between predictive uncertainty, confidence, and calibration <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>.

text.text: ReCaRL incorporates masked supervision for ambiguous labels; the supplied sensitivity analysis additionally examines uncertainty-to-negative, uncertainty-to-positive, and soft-target policies.
Discrimination alone does not establish that predicted probabilities are reliable at a clinical decision threshold.
Calibration and performance under institutional shift therefore complement AUROC and AUPRC.
Research in medical visual question answering has likewise highlighted the value of grounding reasoning in image evidence, although evidence localization differs from disease-label calibration [14].
text.formatted: Research in medical visual question answering has likewise highlighted the value of grounding reasoning in image evidence, although evidence localization differs from disease-label calibration <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>.

text.text: Patient overlap and differences in reference-label definitions may bias external comparisons; these issues should be considered when interpreting the available results [7, 8].
text.formatted: Patient overlap and differences in reference-label definitions may bias external comparisons; these issues should be considered when interpreting the available results <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8]</ref>.

text.text: Multi-institutional chest radiograph studies have also demonstrated that pneumonia classifier performance may change across hospital systems [18].
text.formatted: Multi-institutional chest radiograph studies have also demonstrated that pneumonia classifier performance may change across hospital systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref>.

text.text: This retrospective computational study examined multi-label prediction on chest radiographs using CheXpert for internal model assessment and MIMIC-CXR as an external dataset [1, 2].
text.formatted: This retrospective computational study examined multi-label prediction on chest radiographs using CheXpert for internal model assessment and MIMIC-CXR as an external dataset <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2]</ref>.

text.text: The aggregate results reported below were supplied as study outputs.
Exact patient-level partitions, image eligibility filters, and cohort assembly decisions require confirmation against the original experiment records before public dissemination.
No patient or image counts are inferred from the performance summaries.
The external evaluation was designated as MIMIC-CXR.

Because report-derived findings and image availability may differ across repositories, interpretation of external performance depends on the final mapping of findings and verification of patient-disjoint cohorts.
External performance figures are described below using the supplied evaluation labels; the aggregate tables alone do not document every preprocessing or cohort-selection choice.
The intended target set consists of 12 CheXpert observations excluding "No Finding" and "Support Devices."
The five frequently evaluated findings-atelectasis, cardiomegaly, consolidation, edema, and pleural effusion-are analyzed separately.
These labels describe radiographic findings and are not necessarily equivalent to confirmed etiologic diagnoses.
The distinction between patient-level and image-level splitting is important because repeated studies can create data leakage.
Likewise, studies of graph-based label dependence must separate clinical category membership from correlations estimated on observed labels.
These considerations inform the method specification described below.
For image i and finding k, let y_ik {0, 1, U, M}, where U denotes a report-derived uncertain mention and ∈ M denotes an absent or unusable annotation.
The supervision mask m_ik equals 1 only for definitively positive or negative labels.
The reported sensitivity analysis also considered alternative treatments of U, while the same class definitions were retained.
The model specification uses single-channel chest radiographs resized to 320 × 320 pixels and a
DenseNet121 feature extractor followed by global average pooling and a 12-output classification head.
Intensity normalization, image augmentation, pretrained initialization and view-selection rules affect reproducibility and must be matched to the executed training configuration.
In particular, left-right flipping can alter clinically informative laterality and device placement, and should not be presumed to be a valid augmentation without inspection.
Pairwise relationships are estimated exclusively on the training partition.
For findings j and k with sufficiently many jointly observed binary labels, we compute a prevalence-adjusted phi correlation φ_jk and the support count n_jk.
Negative or unstable correlations are omitted from the primary supportive graph, but their frequencies are documented.
Bootstrap resampling of patients estimates the fraction s_jk of replications in which the association remains positive.
We define a nonnegative reliability-weighted graph as:
Here τ denotes a support-shrinkage hyperparameter and K the maximum number of neighbors retained per finding.
These choices determine how strongly low-support or unstable associations contribute to label propagation.
Their numerical settings cannot be recovered from aggregate evaluation metrics.
Edge reliability depends on class prevalence, the fraction of uncertain annotations, observed pairwise support and the stability of estimated associations under patient-level resampling.
These properties are conceptually distinct from predictive AUROC and AUPRC.
Let z_i be the image embedding, ℓ⁰_ik the independent classifier logit, and p⁰_ik = sigmoid(ℓ⁰_ik).
The base model supplies each finding with a provisional probability.
Strong but uncertain source predictions are less suitable for propagating context, so we weight each source message by c_ij = |2p⁰_ij 1|.
The reliability-aware contextual score and final logit are: r_ik = Σ_(j=Z k) A_kj × c_ij × (2p⁰_ij 1) -ℓ_ik = ℓ⁰_ik + α_k r_ik; p_ik = sigmoid(ℓ_ik)

The nonnegative class-specific α_k is constrained to [0, α_max] using a sigmoid parameterization and is learned jointly with the image encoder. α_max and graph sparsity are tuned on the development/tuning sets.
The model can therefore suppress reliance on a weak relation by learning a small α_k, unlike a mandatory fixed penalty.
The graph message is implemented as a differentiable matrix operation, requiring no separate second-stage network.
An important alternative explanation is that any gain comes merely from additional parameters, so a parameter-matched unweighted-graph baseline is required.
High-level groups serve descriptive rather than causal purposes.

Examples include pulmonary parenchymal findings (lung opacity, consolidation, edema, atelectasis and pneumonia), pleural findings (pleural effusion, pneumothorax and other pleural observations), and cardiac findings (cardiomegaly and enlarged cardiomediastinum).
Group scores are not equivalent to a confirmed etiologic diagnosis.
This construction guarantees that each included child probability does not exceed its corresponding group score, without declaring that one disease causes another.
Group scores should be interpreted as probabilistic summaries of listed findings, not as independently validated clinical diagnoses.
"No Finding" is deliberately not treated as the exact logical complement of the 12 target observations because the dataset labels are incomplete and report-derived.
The primary supervised objective is masked, class-balanced binary cross-entropy, with weights computed on training labels only.
Let w_k denote clipped inverse-frequency class weights.
We optimize:
The supervised objective is masked, class-balanced binary cross-entropy.
Confidence gating acts on labelrelation propagation, whereas temperature scaling is applied after model fitting to adjust probability calibration.
Because temperature scaling is monotonic for each finding, it does not change within-class ranking and cannot by itself increase AUROC [19].
text.formatted: Because temperature scaling is monotonic for each finding, it does not change within-class ranking and cannot by itself increase AUROC <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>.

text.text: The The ablation experiments compared graph weighting, confidence gating and alternative treatments of uncertain labels.
These experiments were evaluated using macro AUROC, macro AUPRC and ECE; the available results are reported in Section 4.
Additional graph-size or initialization sweeps are not described as completed experiments.
Internal and external summaries are interpreted separately.

The reproducibility of the comparison depends on patient-level split manifests, dataset versioning, harmonized label maps, model checkpoints and calibration metadata, none of which can be reconstructed from aggregate performance values alone.
The reported outcomes include macro AUROC, macro AUPRC and Brier score for internal comparisons;
AUROC, AUPRC, ECE and changes in AUROC for external comparisons; five-finding AUROC/AUPRC; and macro discrimination and ECE for ablation experiments.
Larger AUROC and AUPRC values indicate better discrimination; smaller Brier scores and ECE values indicate better calibration.
The reported metrics are descriptive summaries.
External performance is reported on the evaluation labeled as MIMIC-CXR using the study-provided metric summaries.
No additional subgroup, reader-study, or expert-adjudication results are claimed.
The per-finding results are confined to the five findings and metrics for which numerical values were supplied.
In particular, baseline class-wise AUPRC and class prevalence are not inferred from the ReCaRL predictions.
Tables 1-4 present the numerical summaries supplied for the internal, external and ablation evaluations.
Analyses requiring patient-level predictions are not reported here.
ReCaRL (B4) yielded internal macro AUROC 0.821 and macro AUPRC 0.437, compared with 0.812 and 0.423 for the masked/weighted baseline (B1), corresponding to absolute differences of 0.009 and 0.014.
The unweighted graph (B2) obtained AUROC 0.810, whereas the reliability-weighted graph (B3) achieved 0.818.
ReCaRL reached five-finding mean AUROC 0.865 compared with 0.858 for B1 and 0.856 for the reproduced HBCE baseline.
Post-hoc calibration (B5) preserved AUROC and AUPRC while reducing the Brier score from 0.113 to 0.102.
These differences are reported descriptively.
Per-finding AUROC and AUPRC for the five frequently evaluated findings are presented in Table 2.
text.formatted: Per-finding AUROC and AUPRC for the five frequently evaluated findings are presented in Table <ref type="table">2</ref>.

text.text: 2 Performance for five common findings For the five common findings, ReCaRL improved AUROC relative to B1 in each category, with absolute differences ranging from +0.006 to +0.008.
AUROC reached 0.816 for atelectasis, 0.826 for cardiomegaly, 0.855 for consolidation, 0.909 for edema, and 0.919 for pleural effusion.
Corresponding ReCaRL AUPRC values were 0.451, 0.471, 0.183, 0.655, and 0.723.
Because the baseline AUPRC values and class prevalences were not supplied for this comparison, relative precision-recall gains cannot be inferred at the finding level.

Classification performance for five common radiographic findings.
The five-finding mean AUROC is reported separately.
In the external evaluation, ReCaRL achieved macro AUROC 0.799 and macro AUPRC 0.409, compared with 0.789 and 0.392 for B1.
The internal-to-external AUROC change for ReCaRL was 0.022.
External ECE was -0.082 for B4 and 0.061 after calibration (B5), while AUROC and AUPRC remained 0.799 and 0.409.
B3 yielded AUROC 0.793 and AUPRC 0.401.
Changes in discrimination across datasets may arise from differences in prevalence, acquisition, case mix and label definitions.
Since only aggregate metrics were available, the relative contributions of these factors cannot be separated.
The ablation analysis showed sequential changes with reliability weighting and confidence gating: macro
AUROC increased from 0.812 (no graph) to 0.818 (reliability only) and 0.821 (reliability plus gate), while macro AUPRC increased from 0.423 to 0.432 and 0.437.
ECE declined from 0.079 to 0.073 and 0.067.
The unweighted graph yielded AUROC 0.810 and ECE 0.086.
Treating uncertain labels as negative or positive resulted in AUROCs of 0.807 and 0.809, while soft uncertain targets yielded 0.817.
No image-level examples or diagnostic attribution maps are included in the present evaluation.

Such visualizations would not in themselves demonstrate causal reliance on clinically relevant image regions. evaluation does not include prospective deployment, reader-based comparisons or patient-outcome measures, and therefore cannot establish clinical benefit.
In this evaluation, ReCaRL obtained macro AUROC 0.821 and macro AUPRC 0.437 internally and 0.799 and 0.409 externally.
Reliability weighting and confidence gating were associated with modest improvements over the masked/weighted baseline.
Post-hoc calibration reduced internal Brier score and external ECE without altering discrimination.
These findings support further investigation of reliability-aware labelrelation learning but do not establish clinical utility.

The findings distinguish statistical association from categorical clinical structure in chest radiograph classification.
In the reported internal comparison, the reliability-weighted graph improved AUROC from 0.812 to 0.818, and adding source-confidence gating increased it to 0.821.
These modest gains are consistent with the premise that not all observed label associations deserve equal weight.
Importantly, the unweighted graph slightly reduced discrimination relative to the masked/weighted baseline, showing that relation propagation is not inherently beneficial.
The absolute internal gains over the masked/weighted baseline were 0.009 AUROC and 0.014 AUPRC; external AUROC increased by 0.010 relative to B1.
The internal-to-external AUROC decline for ReCaRL was 0.022.
These are modest differences and should not be interpreted as proof of clinically meaningful superiority.

Calibration yielded a clearer numerical change than discrimination after post-hoc scaling: internal Brier score decreased from 0.113 to 0.102, and external ECE from 0.082 to 0.061, while AUROC and AUPRC were unchanged.
Temperature scaling is a post-hoc calibration approach rather than a method for improving rank discrimination [19].
text.formatted: Temperature scaling is a post-hoc calibration approach rather than a method for improving rank discrimination <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>.

text.text: Better calibrated probabilities may aid threshold-based decision support, but neither report-derived labels nor calibration statistics establish clinical diagnosis validity.

Work on reportgrounded segmentation [11], radiographic world modeling [12], and latent visual reasoning [14] emphasizes complementary ways of connecting imaging predictions to evidence; clinical effectiveness remains an open question.
text.formatted: Work on reportgrounded segmentation <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>, radiographic world modeling <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>, and latent visual reasoning <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> emphasizes complementary ways of connecting imaging predictions to evidence; clinical effectiveness remains an open question.

text.text: Results from large pretrained foundation models are not directly comparable with the present comparisons, because the backbone, supervision, data composition and label definitions may differ.
Ark+ and CheXFound focus on learning generalizable representations [4, 5], while the present analysis isolates the influence of label-relation modeling on reported classification outcomes.
text.formatted: Ark+ and CheXFound focus on learning generalizable representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5]</ref>, while the present analysis isolates the influence of label-relation modeling on reported classification outcomes.

text.text: The present results characterize discrimination and calibration but do not quantify downstream changes in clinical decisions or patient outcomes.
Interpretation also depends on details of dataset partitioning and label harmonization that are not contained in the reported aggregate tables.
Several limitations remain.
First, report-derived labels may differ from expert-adjudicated radiographic findings.
Second, incomplete annotations and uncertain labels affect the effective supervision and associations among findings.
Third, association stability does not eliminate confounding, prevalence shift or selection bias, limitations that can undermine cross-institutional generalization [18].
text.formatted: Third, association stability does not eliminate confounding, prevalence shift or selection bias, limitations that can undermine cross-institutional generalization <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref>.
